sessions.title: In Christ
sessions.aim: To move from the image of God shared by every person to the specific new identity given to those united with Christ, the name that holds when the performance fails, and to recover the buried meaning of baptism as the public naming of a self received rather than achieved.
sessions.summary: The image of God settles the worth of every human being, but this session goes further, to the particular identity Scripture says is given to those joined to Christ, because the deepest answer the faith offers to who am I is not a quality inside you but a location outside you. In Christ. Paul's most startling claim about himself is not that he has become his best self but that his old self has died and his life is now hidden somewhere else entirely. I have been crucified with Christ, he writes, it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And, your life is hidden with Christ in God. The first question is whether this means the erasure of the self, losing your individuality into some religious collective, the very crushing of the person the modern self rightly feared. Bell takes that worry at full strength, because it is the strongest objection the age has against the faith on exactly this point. But union with Christ is not erasure, it is the opposite, the self finally given a foundation solid enough to actually be itself, because its worth is no longer riding on its own performance. Then the turn, through baptism, the most underused identity word the church possesses. Baptism is not mainly a ceremony you complete, it is a naming, the public declaration that your identity has been relocated, buried with Christ and raised with him, so that who you are is now anchored in what he did and not in what you do. Luther, in his darkest hours of self-accusation, is said to have steadied himself with three words, I am baptized, not I feel saved or I have performed, but a fact done to him that he could return to when his own performance and his own feelings gave way. The verdict the session reaches is this. There is a name that holds when everything you built collapses, and it is not a name you made. It is a name you were given, in Christ, and it cannot be unfollowed, cancelled, or lost, because the One who holds it never fails.

keyScripture.why: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me, Paul's relocation of identity off the performing self and onto union with Christ, a self that has died to the project of self-justification and now lives by a life and a worth it did not produce.

discussion.q: Paul says the deepest answer to who he is, is not a quality inside him but a location outside him, in Christ. What is the difference between an identity you hold inside yourself and one anchored outside yourself, and why might the outside one be steadier?
discussion.behind: Open on the relocation of identity, which is the heart of the session. An identity held inside the self rises and falls with the self's performance, an identity anchored outside it does not. The aim is to feel why a worth located in Christ is steadier than one located in your own qualities, because it no longer moves when you do.

discussion.q: Paul writes your life is hidden with Christ in God. What would it mean for your truest self to be hidden somewhere safe rather than constantly on display and at stake?
discussion.behind: Press on the word hidden, which is a relief to the performed self. The buffered self has to display everything, with nothing safe. Help the room feel that a hidden identity is not a lost one but a protected one, secure precisely because it is not riding on the visible performance, out of reach of the audience's verdict.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously the fear that union with Christ means losing yourself into a religious collective. Where do you feel the tension between belonging to Christ and remaining genuinely yourself, and how might the two not be opposed?
discussion.behind: Steelman the erasure worry, which is the age's strongest objection here. The aim is to surface the fear honestly and then feel the reversal, that union with Christ is not the dissolving of the self but the grounding of it, the foundation that lets you finally be yourself without your worth at stake. Do not resolve it too fast.

discussion.q: Luther is said to have steadied himself in his worst self-accusation with three words, I am baptized, a fact done to him rather than a feeling he produced. When your own performance and feelings give way, what fact do you return to, and what would it mean to have one?
discussion.behind: Move to the steadying power of a given fact. The performed self has only feelings and performance to fall back on, both of which fail. Help the room feel the difference between an identity grounded in a fact done to you and one grounded in how you are doing, so they sense why baptism is such a sturdy anchor.

discussion.q: Bell says there is a name that holds when everything you built collapses, and it is not a name you made. Where have you watched a self you built collapse, and what would it have changed to have a name underneath it that you could not lose?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication and hope. Everyone has had a built self collapse, a role, an achievement, a relationship that was carrying their identity. Go first. The aim is honest recognition that the selves we make can be lost, and the longing for one that cannot, which is exactly what union with Christ offers, a name that does not collapse.

objections.objection: Losing myself in Christ sounds exactly like the crushing of the individual the modern world fought so hard to escape. You spent the first session defending the protest against being forced into a mold, and now you are telling me to dissolve into a religious identity. That is the mold again.
objections.response: This is the strongest objection in the study and Bell will not dodge it, because it is right to fear the erasure of the person, the faith has sometimes done exactly that, and the protest against it is one the prophets would sign. So hear the actual claim with care, because union with Christ is the reverse of erasure. The self that dies in I have been crucified with Christ is not your personality, your gifts, your particularity, your you. It is specifically the performing self, the self that has to justify its own existence, the exhausting author-and-audience self from session two whose death is the best news you have ever heard. What rises is not a generic religious unit but you, the same you, finally given a foundation solid enough that you can stop defending yourself and actually become who you were made to be. Think about it concretely. The most genuinely individual people you have ever met are usually the ones least anxious about proving their individuality, because their worth is settled and so they are free to be odd, free to be uncool, free to be themselves without managing it. Union with Christ produces exactly that freedom. It does not pour you into a mold. It takes you out of the only mold that was ever really crushing you, the mold of having to earn your own worth, and sets you free to be a self at last.

objections.objection: Telling people their real self is hidden with Christ sounds like a way to avoid dealing with their actual life and problems. It is escapism, retreating into a spiritual identity instead of facing who you really are and the hard work of becoming better.
objections.response: Bell grants that this can be abused, that a person can hide behind spiritual language to avoid the genuine work of change, and the church has enabled that dodge, so the worry is fair. But notice that the reality runs the opposite direction. The reason most people cannot face who they really are, the failures, the patterns, the shameful parts, is that their worth is riding on the verdict, so honest self-examination feels like a threat to their very identity and they flinch from it. The person whose identity is hidden with Christ, settled and safe and not at stake, is the one finally free to look at themselves honestly, because the looking can no longer destroy them. Your worst trait, fully admitted, cannot lower a worth that was never based on your traits. So union with Christ does not let you avoid your actual life, it is the only thing that makes facing your actual life bearable. The performed self has to hide its failures to protect its worth. The self hidden in Christ can confess its failures freely, because the worth is already secured elsewhere. That is not escapism. It is the only foundation from which real honesty and real change are even possible.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your truest self were genuinely hidden with Christ, safe, settled, out of reach of any verdict, what part of your life would you finally be free to face honestly that you have been hiding because facing it felt like it would destroy you?
sessions.practice: This week, learn to return to the fact rather than the feeling. When the performance fails, when you fall short, when the old anxiety about your worth rises, do what Luther is said to have done, return to a fact done to you rather than a state you produced. If you have been baptized, say it, I am baptized, my identity is buried with Christ and raised with him, this is true regardless of how today went. If you have not, return instead to the fact of Christ's finished work for you. Each morning read Colossians 3:3, your life is hidden with Christ in God, and through the day, every time you feel your identity rise or fall with your performance, name the relocation out loud, my life is not here, on display and at stake, it is hidden, safe, in him. Write down what it does to your anxiety to anchor your worth in a fact done to you rather than a performance you are running.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have built so many selves and watched them fall, the role that ended, the achievement that faded, the image that cracked, and each time it felt like we were falling with them, because we were standing on them. We thank you that in Christ you have given us a name we did not make and therefore cannot lose, that our life is hidden with Christ in you, safe, settled, out of reach of the audience and the verdict and even our own failure. Forgive us for living as though our worth were on display when you have hidden it in your Son. When our performance gives way, and it will, teach us to return to the fact, I am yours, baptized into Christ, crucified with him and raised with him, the same self finally given ground to stand on. Let us stop defending a self we built and rest in the one you gave. Amen.
reflection: Is my identity held inside myself, where it rises and falls with my performance, or anchored outside myself in Christ, and how does my anxiety reveal which one I am actually standing on?
What would change if I believed my truest self were hidden with Christ, safe and settled, rather than constantly on display and at stake before the audience?
When my own performance and feelings give way, what fact do I return to, and what would it mean to have a name done to me that I could not perform my way out of or fail my way out of?
sessions.teaching: The image of God, which we sat with last time, is the dignity of every human being, settled at creation, true of every person whether they believe anything or not. Tonight we go further, to the specific new identity the faith says is given to those joined to Christ, and I want to begin with the most startling thing Paul ever wrote about himself, because it cuts directly against everything the age teaches us to want. The age tells us the answer to who am I is a quality we find inside ourselves, the true self, the inner core. Paul says the answer to who he is, is not a quality inside him at all. It is a location outside him. I have been crucified with Christ, he writes to the Galatians. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And to the Colossians, even more strangely, you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Read those slowly, because they are doing something the modern ear can barely process. Paul is not saying he has improved himself, become his best self, found his true inner core. He is saying his old self died, was crucified, is gone, and that his real life, his truest identity, is now located somewhere else entirely, hidden, in Christ, in God. The center of gravity of who he is has moved outside of him. That is the deepest answer the Christian faith gives to the question of identity, and it is not a quality you possess but a union you have been brought into. In Christ. Now I have to stop and take, at full strength, the objection that the modern self will raise here immediately, because it is the strongest objection the age has against the faith on this exact point, and to dodge it would be dishonest. It sounds like erasure. It sounds like exactly the thing the first session honored the protest against, the crushing of the individual into a mold, the dissolving of the person into a collective, the loss of your hard-won self into some religious mass where everyone is the same and no one is anyone. We spent session one defending the refusal to be forced into a slot, and now here is Paul saying it is no longer I who live, which can sound like the slot to end all slots. If that is what union with Christ meant, the modern world would be right to fight it, and I would fight it too. So hear the actual claim, because it is the reverse. The self that dies in I have been crucified with Christ is not your personality. It is not your gifts, your humor, your particularity, the specific and irreplaceable you. It is the performing self. It is the exhausted author-and-audience self from session two, the one that has to justify its own existence, generate its own worth, defend its own standing every single day. That self, and only that self, is what gets crucified, and its death is not a loss, it is the best news in the world, because that self was never the real you, it was the prison you were trapped in. And what rises on the other side of that death is not a generic religious unit with your name filed off. It is you, the same you, for the first time standing on a foundation solid enough that you no longer have to hold yourself up. Here is the thing that proves it. The most genuinely individual, distinctive, unmistakably themselves people you have ever known are almost never the ones working hardest to be individuals. They are the ones who have stopped, the ones whose worth is so settled that they are free to be strange, free to be unimpressive, free to be uncool, free to be exactly who they are without managing the impression, because nothing is riding on it. That freedom is precisely what union with Christ gives. It does not pour you into a mold. It breaks the one mold that was actually crushing you, the mold of having to earn your own worth, and it sets you loose to be a self at last, an unanxious self, because the self is no longer the thing it has to protect. And now hear the word hidden again, because it is a mercy the performed self can barely imagine. Your life is hidden with Christ in God. The buffered, performing self has to put everything on display, has to have its worth visible and verified, nothing safe, nothing out of reach of the verdict. Paul says your truest self is hidden, taken off the stage, placed somewhere the audience cannot reach and the verdict cannot touch and even your own failure cannot get at it, kept safe in God himself. That is not a lost self. It is a protected one. It is your identity moved to the one place where it cannot be cancelled, unfollowed, exposed, or lost, because it is held by Christ and not by your performance. And the church has a word for the moment this relocation is declared, the most underused identity word it owns, and it is baptism. We have shrunk baptism into a ceremony, a thing you complete, a box checked, and in doing so we have lost what it actually is, which is a naming. Baptism is the public declaration that your identity has been relocated, that you have been, as Paul puts it, buried with Christ and raised with him, that who you are is now anchored in what he did and not in what you do. It is not first something you perform. It is first something done to you, a name spoken over you, a fact established about you that does not depend on your feelings about it on a given morning. And this is exactly why it could function as an anchor in the worst storms of the soul. Martin Luther, who battled crushing spells of self-accusation and dread so severe he could barely function, is said to have steadied himself in those hours with three words written where he could see them, I am baptized. Not I feel forgiven, because he often did not. Not I have performed well enough, because he was certain he had not. But I am baptized, a fact done to him, outside him, that remained true when his feelings and his performance had both collapsed, a name he could return to precisely because he had not generated it and therefore could not un-generate it by failing. That is the genius of an identity grounded in a fact rather than a feeling. The feeling fails. The performance fails. The fact, done to you by another, holds. So here is the verdict this session leaves us with, and it is the turn the whole study has been building toward. There is a name that holds when everything you built collapses. You have watched selves collapse, we all have, the role that ended and took your sense of who you were with it, the achievement that faded, the relationship that defined you and then was gone, the image that cracked in front of everyone. And when a self you built collapses, it feels like you are collapsing, because you were standing on it. The promise of union with Christ is that underneath every self you built there can be a name you did not build, a name given to you in Christ, anchored in what he did and not in what you do, hidden safe in God where no failure and no audience and no death can reach it. It cannot be unfollowed. It cannot be cancelled. It cannot be lost, because the One who holds it does not fail, and your life is hidden in him. I have stood on selves that collapsed. I built them out of intellect and argument and the approval of rooms, and I felt them give way and felt myself going down with them, because I had nothing underneath. The thing that finally held was not a better self I managed to build. It was a name I was given, a fact done to me, a life relocated into Christ and hidden there. And when I fail now, and I do, I am learning, slowly, to do what Luther did, to stop reaching for a feeling or a performance to save me and to return instead to the fact. I am his. That holds. It is the only thing that ever has.

scriptureStudy.note: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Identity is relocated off the performing self and onto union with Christ, the old self-justifying self dead and a new life received rather than produced.

For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. The truest self is hidden, safe, out of reach of the audience and the verdict, secure precisely because it is not riding on the visible performance.

All of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death, buried with him, so that we too might walk in newness of life. Baptism is the naming of a relocated identity, buried and raised with Christ, a fact done to us.

If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away, behold, the new has come. The phrase in Christ marks the location of the new identity, given and not achieved, the old performing self gone and a new self received.

He chose us in him before the foundation of the world, he predestined us for adoption. The new identity is grounded in God's choice before we existed, the deepest possible foundation, settled before any performance could affect it.

But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession. Identity is named in the plural and conferred by God's choosing, a status given, belonging that grounds the self rather than dissolving it.

To the one who conquers I will give a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it. The final identity is a name given by Christ, known to the receiver, the deepest self bestowed rather than self-constructed.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the doctrine of union with Christ, because it is the rich center of Paul's theology of identity and the modern church has often let it shrink into sentiment. The phrase in Christ and its variants appear well over a hundred times in Paul's letters, and they are not decorative, they name the structural reality of the Christian's existence, that the believer's standing, righteousness, life, and identity are not qualities the believer possesses in themselves but realities held in Christ and shared by union with him. The Reformers, especially Calvin, made this the engine of the whole gospel, that everything Christ accomplished is of no benefit to us until we are united to him, so that our righteousness is not our own achievement but his, received by faith and held in him, which is precisely why it cannot be lost by our failure or earned by our performance. A serious group should see how directly this answers the exhaustion the study has been tracing. The performed self must generate and defend its own worth because that worth is located in itself, on display, at stake. Union with Christ relocates the worth entirely, so that it is held in another, secure in him, and therefore not riding on the believer's daily performance at all. Set this beside the modern buffered self and feel the depth of the alternative. The buffered self is sealed off and self-contained, drawing meaning from within its own walls, and union with Christ is the dismantling of exactly that wall, the self opened up and grounded outside itself in another, which the buffered self would experience as a threat and which is in fact its rescue. Weigh too the recovery of baptism as the sign and seal of this union, not a work the believer performs but a word God speaks, a fact done to them that functions, as it did for Luther, as an anchor when feeling and performance fail. The discipline is to learn to think of yourself the way Paul thinks of himself, not as a self you must construct and defend but as a self united to Christ, hidden in God, your worth held safe in another and therefore finally, restfully, your own.

memoryVerse.text: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

sessions.title: The Self Poured Out
sessions.aim: To end where the whole study has been heading, with the paradox that the self is found by being lost, and to show that an identity secure enough not to need defending is finally free to be spent in love rather than performed for approval, the difference between a self poured out and a self performed.
sessions.summary: The study ends on the hardest and most freeing word Jesus ever spoke about the self. Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. This is the exact reverse of everything the age teaches. The age says save the self, build it, protect it, express it, put it first. Jesus says the self you clutch and protect is the self you lose, and the self you give away is the self you find. The first question is whether this is just spiritual self-erasure, a call to a doormat existence of having no self at all, which is what the modern ear hears and rightly resists. Bell takes that worry at full strength, because losing yourself can sound like exactly the codependent self-abandonment that wounds people. But the losing Jesus means is not the erasure of the self, it is the relaxing of the grip, and only a self that is already secure can possibly let go. This is why the whole study had to come first. You cannot pour out a self you are still desperately trying to fill. The performed self cannot afford to lose itself, it has nothing underneath, so every act of service is secretly another performance, another bid for approval. But a self whose worth is already settled in Christ, hidden and safe, can finally be spent without fear, because there is nothing left to protect. The turn is the deepest reversal of the study. The self-made age produces a self that must be performed, anxiously, for an audience, forever. The given identity produces a self that can be poured out, freely, in love, because it has stopped needing anything from anyone. The study does not end with a self admired. It ends with a self spent, and finds, against everything the age believes, that the spent self is the only one that was ever truly free, and truly found.

keyScripture.why: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it, Jesus' direct reversal of the self-saving age, naming the secured self as the one free to be spent and the clutched self as the one that is lost.

discussion.q: Jesus says whoever would save his life will lose it, the exact reverse of the age, which says save the self, protect it, put it first. Where have you experienced that clutching a self tightly actually cost you the very thing you were trying to keep?
discussion.behind: Open on the great reversal in lived experience. Most have seen that grasping for security loses it, in a relationship, a reputation, a control. The aim is to feel the paradox is not abstract but observable, that the self-protective move backfires, so the room is ready to hear why the given-away self is the found one.

discussion.q: The session says you cannot pour out a self you are still desperately trying to fill. Why does the whole study have to come first before this last word, and what happens when people try to lose themselves before their worth is secure?
discussion.behind: Establish why security must precede sacrifice. People who serve from an empty, unsecured self are still performing, still bidding for approval, and they burn out or grow resentful. Help the room see that genuine self-giving is only possible from a self already settled in Christ, which is why this session is last, not first.

discussion.q: Bell takes seriously that losing yourself can sound like codependent self-abandonment, the doormat with no self at all. How is the losing Jesus means different from that, and why does the difference matter?
discussion.behind: Steelman the self-erasure worry, which is real and pastorally serious. The aim is to distinguish the relaxing of the grip on a secure self from the abandonment of a self that was never secure, the first freedom and the second a wound. Protect anyone in the room who has been spiritually pressured into self-erasure, and name the difference clearly.

discussion.q: The session says a performed self cannot afford to lose itself because it has nothing underneath, so even its service is secretly another performance. Where have you served or given in a way that was secretly a bid for approval, and how did you know?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, gently. Much of our giving is performance in disguise, service that needs to be seen and thanked. Go first. The aim is honest recognition that unsecured giving is still about the self, not a guilt trip, so people feel why only a secured self can give freely, without keeping score.

discussion.q: The study ends not with a self admired but a self spent, and claims the spent self is the only one truly free and truly found. As you look back over the five sessions, what would it actually change about your week to live from a given identity rather than a performed one?
discussion.behind: Close the whole study by integrating it into the ordinary week. The aim is to move all five sessions from idea to life, to have each person name one concrete way a secured, given identity would change how they live, work, serve, and rest. Let it land as invitation, not assignment, and leave weight rather than tying a bow.

objections.objection: Lose your life and pour yourself out sounds like a recipe for being used up, for letting everyone walk over you, for having no boundaries and no self. People have been spiritually abused with exactly this verse, told to sacrifice themselves into the ground. Why is this not just codependence with a Bible verse?
objections.response: Bell will not wave this away, because the verse has been weaponized, used to push the abused back into danger and to shame people out of legitimate self-protection, and anyone in the room who has been wounded that way deserves to hear it named as the abuse it was, not the teaching of Jesus. So hear the crucial distinction. There is a world of difference between losing a self that is secure and abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. The codependent self-abandonment that destroys people is not the free pouring out of a settled self, it is the desperate emptying of an unsettled one, a person with no foundation trying to earn worth or safety by disappearing, which is not love but fear wearing love's clothes. That is why this is the last session and not the first. You cannot freely lose a self until you have a self secure enough to lose, hidden safe in Christ, its worth already settled, nothing left to protect by grasping. The doormat has no self underneath and is being erased. The saint has a self so secure it can be spent without being lost, because the worth is held in Christ and cannot be drained by anyone. Losing your life in Jesus' sense requires first having found it in him. The order is everything, and reversing it is the abuse.

objections.objection: This whole study built up to a secure, settled identity, and now you are telling me to give it away. That feels like a bait and switch. You spent four sessions convincing me my worth is safe and now you want me to spend it on other people. Why would I let go of the very security you just gave me?
objections.response: It would be a bait and switch if security were the destination, but it was never the destination, it was the foundation, and that distinction is the whole point. The age treats a secure self as the goal, the finish line, the thing to achieve and then enjoy, which leaves you with a settled self that turns inward and admires itself, and a self that exists only to enjoy its own security is, in the end, a small and lonely thing. Notice that you do not let go of the security by pouring yourself out, you exercise it. The reason you can spend yourself on others without fear is precisely that the worth is settled in Christ and cannot be drained, so giving it away does not lower it. A self that has to protect its worth has to hoard it, can never risk it on love, and stays curved in on itself. A self whose worth is secure in Christ is the only self that can afford to forget itself, to be spent, to love without keeping score, because nothing it gives can cost it what was never riding on the giving. The security is not for hoarding. It is the very thing that makes self-forgetful love possible at last, and a self-forgetful love is the freest and most found a human being ever is. You are not being asked to give back the gift. You are being shown what the gift was for.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If your worth were so settled in Christ that you genuinely had nothing left to protect, who is the one person, and what is the one act of love, you would pour yourself into that you have been holding back because you could not afford to?
sessions.practice: This week, practice the one move only a secured self can make, self-forgetful love that keeps no score. Choose one act of genuine self-giving, toward a person who cannot repay it or thank you adequately, and do it without telling anyone, without being seen, with no return possible, precisely to feel the difference between serving for approval and serving from security. Watch the part of you that wants credit, and instead of feeding it, return to the fact that your worth is already settled in Christ and does not need this to be seen. Each morning read Mark 8:35 and Galatians 2:20 together, the losing and the union, and ask where you can spend a self that cannot be drained. Looking back over all five sessions, write down the one concrete way you most want to live from a given identity rather than a performed one, and name the first step.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we came into this study tired of building a self, and you have shown us a self we did not have to build, made in your image, given in Christ, hidden safe in you, a name we cannot lose. And now, at the end, you ask the hardest and most freeing thing, that we let it go, not because it is not precious but because it is so secure that it can finally be spent. Teach us the difference between losing a self that is safe in you and abandoning one that was never secure, and protect the ones in this room who have been wounded by that confusion. Free us from the giving that is secretly a performance, the love that keeps score, the service that needs to be seen. Settle our worth so deeply in your Son that we forget ourselves at last, and pour ourselves out, and discover, against everything the age told us, that the self we gave away was the only one we ever truly found. Not the self we were sold. The self you gave. Amen.
reflection: Where has clutching a self tightly, to save it, protect it, or prove it, actually cost me the very thing I was trying to keep, and what would it mean to loosen the grip?
How much of my serving and giving has been a performance in disguise, a bid for approval rather than self-forgetful love, and what does the difference reveal about where my worth is anchored?
Looking back over all five sessions, what would actually change about my ordinary week if I lived from an identity given to me in Christ rather than one I have to perform for an audience?
sessions.teaching: We end where the whole study has been heading, and we end on the hardest and most freeing thing Jesus ever said about the self, a sentence that runs directly against everything the age has trained us to believe. Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. Hear how completely that reverses the instruction we have lived under. The age says save the self. Build it, protect it, express it, put it first, guard it against anyone who would diminish it, because the self is the one thing you have and losing it is the great catastrophe. Jesus says the exact opposite. The self you clutch and protect and try to save is precisely the self you will lose, and the self you give away, lose, spend, pour out, is the one you will find. The whole logic of the self-made age is stood on its head in a single sentence. Now I have to take, at full and serious strength, the objection the modern ear raises here, because it is not a cheap objection, it is a wound, and there are people in any room who carry it. Lose your life sounds like self-erasure. It sounds like the call to have no self at all, to become a doormat, to abandon yourself, to let everyone walk over you in the name of holiness, to disappear. And here I have to be careful and honest, because this verse has been weaponized. It has been used to push abused people back into danger, to shame the wounded out of any self-protection, to tell the person being destroyed that their destruction is godly. That is not the teaching of Jesus. That is spiritual abuse wearing his words, and if anyone in this room has been hurt that way, hear me plainly, that was a lie told to you, and Jesus never said it. So we have to draw the distinction that the whole thing turns on, and it is this. There is an infinite difference between losing a self that is secure and abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. The codependent self-abandonment that destroys people, the disappearing, the having no boundaries, the letting yourself be erased, is not the free pouring out of a settled self. It is the desperate emptying of an unsettled one. It is a person with no foundation trying to buy worth or safety by vanishing, which is not love at all, it is fear in love's clothing, and it leaves the person more enslaved, not more free. That is not what the secured self does. And this is the whole reason this session comes last and not first. This is why we could not start here. You cannot freely lose a self until you have, first, found a self secure enough to be lost. You cannot pour out a self you are still desperately trying to fill. Think about it. The performed self from session two, the buffered self with no ground but its own performance, simply cannot afford to lose itself, because it has nothing underneath, no foundation in reserve. So every act of so-called service from that self is secretly another performance, another bid for the approval it needs to survive, another way of building the self while appearing to give it away. The unsecured self cannot give. It can only invest, hoping for a return, because it is too poor to spend anything for free. This is why so much religious service curdles into resentment and burnout, because it was never self-forgetful love, it was the performed self trying to earn its worth through good deeds, keeping a secret ledger, needing to be seen and thanked, and a self that needs to be thanked has not given anything, it has made a purchase. And I know that ledger, because I have kept it. I have served and needed it noticed. I have given and waited for the credit. I have done the right thing and felt the quiet resentment when no one saw, which is the surest sign that the giving was about me, that I was performing love rather than pouring it out, because love poured out from a secure self does not keep score, and mine was counting. But here is the turn, the deepest reversal in the whole study, and it is genuinely good news. A self whose worth is already settled, hidden safe in Christ, anchored in what he did and not what it does, can finally be spent without fear, because there is nothing left to protect. When your worth is secure in Christ and cannot be drained, then giving yourself away does not diminish you, because what you are giving is not your security, your security is held in another, untouchable. So you are free, for the first time, to actually love, to forget yourself, to be poured out, to serve the person who cannot repay you and will not thank you, to do the good thing in secret with no return possible, because you no longer need anything from anyone. The secured self is the only self that can afford to forget itself. That is the freedom the whole study has been building toward. And do not miss that this is exactly the shape of Christ himself, who, Paul says, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, poured himself out, all the way to a cross. He could pour himself out completely because his identity was completely secure, the eternally beloved Son, and a worth that settled has nothing to defend and so everything to give. He is the self poured out, and union with him is what makes the same pouring out possible, slowly, in us. So here is where the study ends, and I will not tie it in a bow, because the last word is not a conclusion but an invitation that costs something. We came in tired of building a self, sold the lie that we had to invent ourselves, look inward, perform, and win the room's approval forever, and we found it was a kind of slavery dressed as freedom. We found that the deepest thing about us was given, not chosen, that we are made in God's image and our worth was settled at creation, that in Christ we are given a name we cannot lose, hidden safe in God. And now, at the very end, we find that the point of all this security was never to have a secure self to admire. The point was to have a self secure enough to spend. The self-made age produces a self that must be performed, anxiously, for an audience, forever, and never finds itself. The given identity produces a self that can be poured out, freely, in love, and finds, in the pouring, the thing it was looking for all along. This study does not end with a self admired. It ends with a self spent. And the last word, the one I want you to carry out of here, is the one the age cannot believe and Jesus swore was true. The self you finally stop clutching, the self you let go of because it is already safe in him, the self you pour out in love without keeping score, is not the self you lose. It is the only self you ever truly find. Not the self you were sold. The self you were given, and then, freely, gave away.

scriptureStudy.note: Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it. The great reversal, the self clutched is lost and the self spent is found, naming the secured self as the one finally free to be poured out.

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit. The pattern of fruitfulness through self-giving, the self that protects itself remains alone, the self poured out bears life.

Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. Christ pours himself out from total security in his identity as the Son, the model of a secured self spent in love, which union with him makes possible in us.

It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. The union that grounds the pouring out, the self spent in love is not self-erasure but Christ's own self-giving life expressed through a self secured in him.

What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Jesus exposes the self-saving project as the very thing that loses the self, the gaining that is really a forfeiting, the clutching that ends in loss.

My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. The secure self can embrace weakness without threat, because its worth is held in Christ and not in its own strength, freeing it from the need to perform competence.

By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. Self-giving love is grounded in Christ's prior self-giving, the pattern of the poured-out self flowing from the love that secured us first.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the paradox of self-fulfillment through self-forgetfulness, because it is the deepest collision between the gospel and the self-made age, and it is more than a pious slogan, it is a claim about how the self actually works. The age operates on a simple assumption, that the way to a fulfilled self is to attend to the self, build it, express it, prioritize it, and that turning toward others is a cost the self pays, a subtraction from its own flourishing. Jesus and the whole Christian tradition claim the opposite, that the self curved in on itself, attending always to its own state and worth, is the unhappy self, and that the self is paradoxically found, fulfilled, made glad, precisely in self-forgetfulness, in attention turned outward toward God and neighbor. The medieval description of sin as the heart curved in on itself names the disease, a self so preoccupied with itself that it cannot rest, cannot love freely, cannot get out of its own way, which is exactly the condition the performed self of session two lives in, endlessly monitoring its own reception. A serious group should weigh how this reframes the whole study. The point of a secure identity in Christ is not to produce a self that finally feels good about itself, a kind of holy self-esteem, because a self still focused on its own feeling about itself, even a positive feeling, is still curved inward. The point is a self so secure that it is finally free to stop thinking about itself at all, to forget itself in love, which is the only condition in which a human being is actually at rest and actually glad. Set this against the modern therapeutic project of building self-esteem and ask whether the endless work of feeling good about oneself is not just another form of the exhausting self-focus the study has diagnosed, and whether the gospel offers something deeper than higher self-regard, namely freedom from the need to regard the self at all. The discipline is to see that the security Christ gives is not the destination but the doorway, that an identity received and not performed exists finally so that the self can be spent, poured out, forgotten in love, and that this self-forgetfulness, which the age fears as self-loss, is in fact the only place the self has ever truly been found.

memoryVerse.text: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it.

leaderPrimer: Every small group is an audience, and an audience is exactly what the people in this study do not need one more of. They live before audiences all day, the feed, the workplace, the mirror, the merciless inner critic keeping score, and the hazard of these five weeks is that your circle of chairs quietly becomes another stage. Watch for it. Someone will confess their exhaustion with performing in a way that is itself a performance, polished, likable, well timed, and you must not reward the polish. Reward the fumble instead. The half sentence that goes nowhere, the admission that arrives ugly, the person who says they do not actually know who they are, that is the study working, and the room must learn that nobody here is grading. It learns that from you, which is inconvenient, because leading is a performed role too, and you will feel the pull to be impressive about a study on the tyranny of being impressive. Refuse it in the first ten minutes. Bell spent years building a self with no God in the picture, an atheist manufacturing his own foundation, and he was raised without a father, so the question of who he was had a hole where an inherited name should have sat. He has performed a self he was not sure was real and gone home empty from rooms that applauded it. When he says the self we were sold is exhausting, that is autobiography, and yours should join it early. Be gentle with the steelman in session one. The instruction to be true to yourself is not stupid, it was liberation from real tyrannies, and half your room got free of something through it, so honor that before the study counts its costs, or nobody will trust the counting. And be patient in the turn to gift. People who have carried the project of themselves for decades do not set it down on a Tuesday because Galatians was mentioned. They set it down in rooms where, for one hour, nothing they say is being scored. Build that hour. Let your group be the one place all week where every person is off the market. No selling here. Nothing to audition for. That hour is the study.

faq.q: Is this study going to make me feel guilty about how much I curate and perform myself?
faq.a: No, and it works hard to prevent exactly that. The whole series is built on the conviction that the performed self is not a character flaw but the reasonable behavior of a person who has been told their worth is something they generate and display, and the leader primer explicitly tells the facilitator that if anyone leaves more ashamed of their performed self than when they came, the study failed. The writer puts himself inside the struggle from the start, admitting he came to faith from atheism and built a self with no God in the picture, that he has measured his worth by the room's reaction and driven home empty, that he has performed a self he was not sure was real and kept a secret ledger on his own good deeds. If you came braced to be told you are vain, you will find instead a study that stands in the exhaustion with you and treats your tiredness as the honest starting place, not the failure.

faq.q: What does it mean that the modern self was invented? Is not the self just what a person is?
faq.a: Session one walks through this carefully. The claim is not that human beings are new but that a particular way of understanding the self is recent, the inward, self-defining individual who looks inside for the answer to who they are and treats their feelings as the truest thing about them. Charles Taylor traces how the West came to experience the self as buffered, sealed off from God and any larger order, drawing its meaning from inside its own boundaries, and Robert Bellah named the working faith of that self, expressive individualism, the belief that each person has a unique inner core to discover and express. The point is not that this is simply wrong but that it is one answer, recent and contestable, to the question of who we are, not the obvious fact of nature we assume it to be. Once you can see that the inward turn is a habit you were trained into rather than a given, you can ask whether there is a deeper foundation underneath it, which is where the rest of the study goes.

faq.q: Be true to yourself is good advice, is not it? Why would a study question it?
faq.a: The study grants what is genuinely good in it before questioning anything, and session one insists on the steelman first. Be true to yourself carries a real and precious protest, the refusal to be crushed into a mold by family or church or culture, the defense of the person against the machine, the dignity of the one irreplaceable life that was told to be quiet and disappear. That protest is closer to the prophets than its critics usually realize, and the study honors it fully. The question it raises is not whether the self matters but which self you are being told to be true to, because if the inward self was itself shaped, all the way down, by the same culture that told you to go looking inside, then being true to it is not standing on bedrock, it is standing on a floor someone built and calling it the ground. The study does not despise the instruction. It asks whether it can bear the weight it has been given.

faq.q: Why is being yourself so exhausting? I thought it was supposed to be freeing.
faq.a: Session two is built on exactly this question. Being told to invent yourself sounds like freedom until you realize there is no final version, the self has to be continually built, defended, updated, and presented, and then, because a self with no foundation outside itself cannot validate itself, you have to anxiously watch the audience to see whether it is landing. So you become two people at once, the author writing the self and the audience watching to see if it sells, and both jobs run all day with no shift change. The exhaustion is not a sign you are doing it badly, it is the built-in cost of a self that has to be earned and re-earned every day and collapses the moment the audience looks away. The study names that tiredness as a message, the honest report of a soul built to be given an identity and trying instead to manufacture one, which it cannot, and was never meant to.

faq.q: If my worth comes from being made in God's image, is not that just a higher standard I have to live up to?
faq.a: Session three answers this directly, because the church has often preached it that way and the worry is fair. But the image of God is not a goal set in front of you to strive toward, it is a status conferred at creation, true of you before you had done anything, good or bad, and true of you on your worst day. You do not earn the image by behaving like God's representative, you bear it because God made you to, and no performance can raise you up to it and no failure can knock you out of it. That is not a higher bar, it is the removal of the bar from the question of your worth entirely. Your dignity was settled at creation by God's act, not computed fresh each morning from the day's results. A gift you must live up to has been turned back into a wage, which is precisely the trap the doctrine was meant to free you from.

faq.q: Does losing yourself in Christ mean losing your individuality, becoming a generic religious person?
faq.a: Session four takes this worry at full strength, because it is the strongest objection the modern world has against the faith on this point, and the answer is the reverse of what the fear assumes. The self that dies in Paul's I have been crucified with Christ is not your personality, your gifts, your particularity, it is specifically the performing self, the one that has to justify its own existence and earn its own worth every day. What rises is not a generic religious unit but you, the same you, finally given a foundation solid enough that you can stop defending yourself and actually become who you were made to be. The most genuinely distinctive people you have ever met are usually the ones least anxious about proving their individuality, because their worth is settled and so they are free to be themselves. Union with Christ does not pour you into a mold, it breaks the one mold that was actually crushing you, the mold of having to earn your own worth.

faq.q: What does baptism have to do with identity?
faq.a: Session four recovers baptism as the most underused identity word the church possesses. We have shrunk it into a ceremony you complete, a box checked, and lost what it actually is, a naming, the public declaration that your identity has been relocated, buried with Christ and raised with him, so that who you are is anchored in what he did and not in what you do. It is first something done to you, a name spoken over you, a fact established that does not depend on your feelings about it on a given morning. That is exactly why it can anchor the soul in its worst storms. Martin Luther, in his crushing spells of self-accusation, is said to have steadied himself with three words, I am baptized, not I feel forgiven, because he often did not, but a fact done to him that held when his feelings and his performance had both collapsed. An identity grounded in a fact done to you holds when one grounded in how you are doing cannot.

faq.q: The study builds toward a secure identity and then session five tells me to give it away. Is not that a bait and switch?
faq.a: It would be, if security were the destination, but it was never the destination, it was the foundation, and session five turns on that distinction. The age treats a secure self as the goal, which leaves you with a settled self that turns inward and admires itself, a small and lonely thing. The study claims the security was always for something, that a self whose worth is settled in Christ and cannot be drained is the only self that can afford to forget itself, to be spent in love without keeping score, because nothing it gives can cost it what was never riding on the giving. You do not let go of the security by pouring yourself out, you exercise it. A self that has to protect its worth has to hoard it and stays curved in on itself, while a self secure in Christ is free at last to love self-forgetfully. The security is not for hoarding, it is the very thing that makes self-forgetful love possible.

faq.q: I have heard lose your life used to pressure people into self-abandonment. How is this different?
faq.a: Session five names that abuse plainly and refuses it. The verse has been weaponized, used to push the abused back into danger and to shame people out of legitimate self-protection, and anyone hurt that way was hurt by an abuse of the verse, not by Jesus, who never said it. The crucial distinction is between losing a self that is secure and abandoning a self that was never secure, and only the first is what Jesus means. The codependent self-abandonment that destroys people is not the free pouring out of a settled self, it is the desperate emptying of an unsettled one, a person with no foundation trying to earn worth or safety by disappearing, which is fear in love's clothing. That is exactly why this is the last session and not the first. You cannot freely lose a self until you have found one secure enough to lose, hidden safe in Christ. The doormat is being erased, the saint is spending a self that cannot be drained. The order is everything, and reversing it is the abuse.

faq.q: I am a skeptic. Is not given identity just a comforting story to replace a harder truth?
faq.a: It is a fair challenge, and session three answers it head on rather than dodging it. The study grants that you cannot prove the image of God the way you prove a theorem, and it will not pretend the claim is a deduction. But it points out that the alternative is in exactly the same position, self-made identity is also a framework, also unproven, also a story, with a specific and testable consequence, that the self has no ground but its own construction and therefore can give you no rest. So the real question is not which story is provable, neither is, but which story fits the evidence of your own life, including the restlessness no achievement quiets and the emptiness on the far side of the applause. The self-made story has no account of that exhaustion except that you have not built well enough yet. The given story does, it says you are tired because you were made to be held and have been trying to hold yourself. The writer came to faith from atheism, so he is not naive about the doubt, he lived it, and he asks you to weigh the stories honestly, not to pretend.

faq.q: Why does the study keep putting the writer and the leader inside the problem instead of just teaching people the answer?
faq.a: Because that is the method, and the method is the mercy. The whole study is about the end of performance, so a leader who performs a settled identity he does not have has already contradicted the message and made the leading itself one more performance. The writer does not stand outside this as the man who has identity mastered, explaining it to the lost. He came to faith from atheism and built a self on sand. He was raised without a father, with a hole where an inherited name should have been. He has measured his worth by the room and gone home empty, clutched selves that collapsed and fallen with them. He writes from inside the exhaustion, and the study asks every leader to lead from there too, because you cannot lead a tired, performing person out of the trap from above without your help curdling into either shame or distance. A leader who admits I perform too, I clutch selves that collapse too, can sit beside the room as a fellow learner, which is the only place real teaching about identity comes from.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have not got my own identity figured out?
faq.a: Your unsettled identity is not a disqualification, it may be your best qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow learner, not by someone who has his worth all settled and now dispenses security to the anxious, and every discussion question carries the answer behind it, every objection is steelmanned and answered, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice, so you are not improvising. Your honesty about where your own worth still rides on the room, the work, or the role may be the most freeing thing in the room, the permission that lets others stop performing. What you do need is to refuse to shame anyone for how much they perform or how lost they feel, to keep the room safe for the exhausted and the collapsed and the skeptical, to protect the wounded especially in session five, to grant the skeptic the strongest form of their objection, and to point everyone, yourself first, to the One who made us in his image and gives us a name in Christ we cannot lose. Read the leader primer, be honest with God about your own performing, and trust the material.

timeline.event: The opening of Genesis, set down in Israel's Scriptures, grounds human identity not in self-definition but in being made in the image of God, the foundational claim that the deepest thing about a person is given at creation, which the study returns to as the floor beneath the modern self.

Paul writes to the Galatians and Romans, framing identity as union with Christ, I have been crucified with Christ, it is no longer I who live, and grounding the new self not in self-construction but in being joined to Christ and named in baptism, the relocation of identity off the performing self.

Paul writes to the Colossians that your life is hidden with Christ in God, naming the truest self as hidden, safe, and secured in Christ rather than on display and at stake, the seam of the study's account of an identity that cannot be cancelled or lost.

Augustine writes the Confessions, the first great autobiography of a self that tried to make itself and failed, and prays you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you, naming the restlessness of the self-made life as a homing signal toward a rest it cannot manufacture.

Martin Luther, battling crushing spells of self-accusation and dread, recovers the believer's identity as a gift received rather than a performance achieved, and is remembered for steadying himself in his darkest hours with the fact done to him, I am baptized, rather than any feeling he could produce.

John Calvin, in the Institutes, makes union with Christ the engine of the gospel, teaching that everything Christ accomplished is of no benefit until we are united to him, so that the believer's righteousness and identity are held in Christ rather than achieved in themselves, the doctrinal spine of session four.

Robert Bellah and his colleagues publish Habits of the Heart, naming the working faith of the modern American self as expressive individualism, the conviction that each person has a unique inner core to discover and express, which informs the study's account of the self-made age.

Charles Taylor publishes A Secular Age, describing the immanent frame and the buffered self, the modern self sealed off from God and any larger order and drawing its meaning from inside its own boundaries, the central diagnostic the study uses to make the modern self visible as an invention.

The rise of the social feed industrializes the performed self, turning the audience's verdict into a visible, countable, real-time number and intensifying the anxious self-validation that was always part of the buffered self, the cultural condition the study addresses as the latest form of an ancient hunger.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. Thank you for being here, and thank you for the honesty it takes, because there is almost nothing harder to talk about truthfully than the self we have been building and defending. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can say I do not really know who I am underneath all this here. You can say my whole worth is riding on my work, or I got everything I performed for and felt nothing, or I am exhausted by being myself. Nobody is going to grade you or hand you a tip to fix it. Second, this study is not a better technique for building a stronger self. It is the discovery that you were made and named before you ever started building, that your worth was given, not earned, and cannot be lost. Third, the writer puts himself inside all of this, and so will I. I have measured my worth by the reaction in a room and gone home empty. I have performed a self I was not sure was real. We are not teaching identity from above. We are being un-made and re-made together. Tonight we are sitting with this part of the question who am I: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we will sit with it before we say anything else. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes, only honest ones.
facilitatorScript.transition: We have looked hard at what this part of the question says about who we are. Now let us bring it home, off the page and into the ordinary week we are about to walk into, into the work and the rooms and the quiet moments where we actually build or set down a self, because that is where this either matters or it does not.
facilitatorScript.close: We are going to stop there, and if it does not feel resolved, that is honest, because an identity received and spent is the work of a life, not a single evening, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. Take this part of the question into your week. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if you carry a self that has already collapsed, or a worth riding on something that cannot hold it, or a wound from being told that having no self was holiness, please do not carry it alone, talk to me or to someone safe in this room. Let me pray for us before we go, because this study practices what it teaches, and ends not in advice but in prayer. Thank you for the honesty it took to be in this room.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and shame, and name plainly that everyone in the room has been building a self and is more tired than they admit, and that this room is safe for that.
Week 2: Session 1, The Buffered Self, full discussion and practice, with extended care to steelman be true to yourself before questioning it, especially for the skeptic.
Week 3: Session 2, The Exhausting Project of Self-Creation, with extended time on the performed self and the audience, handled without contempt because the leader is inside it too.
Week 4: Session 3, Given, Not Chosen, the image of God and identity as gift, with the recovery of Augustine's restless heart as a homing signal rather than a defect.
Week 5: Session 4, part one, In Christ, sitting first with the relocation of identity off the performing self and onto union with Christ, before turning to baptism.
Week 6: Session 4 continued, the baptismal identity, the name done to you that holds when feeling and performance give way, with extended time on Luther's I am baptized.

Week 7: Session 5, The Self Poured Out, found by losing it, handled with great care for those wounded by self-erasure, naming clearly the difference between losing a secure self and abandoning an unsecured one.
Week 8: Integration. Walk back through all five movements, revisit the five practices, and name what each person is carrying out of the study, with space for anyone needing further help.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the invented self and the exhaustion of performing it.
Week 2: Session 3, Given, Not Chosen, the image of God and identity as gift, with extended time on Augustine's restless heart.
Week 3: Session 4, In Christ, union with Christ and the baptismal identity, handled with care for those whose built selves have collapsed.
Week 4: Session 5, The Self Poured Out, found by losing it, plus a short close walking back through all five movements together.

plan: Week 2: Session 2, The Exhausting Project of Self-Creation.
Week 5: Session 5, The Self Poured Out.

glossary.definition: Charles Taylor's term for the modern self sealed off from God, cosmos, and any larger order, drawing its meaning from inside its own boundaries rather than from a world it is embedded in. The study treats it as an invention, not the natural human condition.

Taylor's name for the modern experience of the world as a closed natural system with no window onto anything above or beyond it, so that meaning, if there is any, must come from inside the frame. The condition that makes looking inward seem like the only option.

The working faith of the modern self, named by Robert Bellah, the conviction that each person has a unique inner core of feeling and intuition that must be discovered and expressed, and that doing so is the whole point of a life.

The Genesis claim that the human being is made in God's image, understood in the study not as a standard to perform but as a status conferred at creation, a dignity given before any achievement and unable to be earned or lost.

Augustine's account of the soul's chronic dissatisfaction, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you, read in the study as a homing signal pointing toward a rest the self cannot manufacture and can only receive.

The study's central claim that the deepest thing about a person is given, not chosen, received from God in creation and in Christ rather than assembled by the self, which cannot be earned without ceasing to be a gift.

The self with no foundation outside its own performance, which must be continually built, defended, and presented to an audience whose verdict it needs to feel real, the source of the exhaustion the study diagnoses in session 2.

Paul's structural account of Christian identity, in Christ, the believer's standing, life, and worth held not in themselves but in Christ and shared by union with him, so that identity is located outside the self and cannot be lost by the self's failure.

Identity grounded in baptism understood as a naming, a fact done to the believer that they are buried with Christ and raised with him, an anchor that holds when feeling and performance fail, as in Luther's I am baptized.

The self that, secure in Christ, is finally free to be spent in self-forgetful love rather than performed for approval, the found self of Mark 8:35, which is discovered by being given away rather than clutched and protected.

The freedom of a self so secure in Christ that it can stop attending to its own worth and turn outward in love, the opposite of the self curved in on itself, the only condition in which the study claims the self is truly at rest.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The age handed everyone a single instruction and called it freedom. Look inward, find your true self, define yourself on your own terms, and then perform that self for the world's approval. For many it has become a sentence to hard labor, the work of being your own author and your own audience at once, with no day off and no final version. This five-session study walks through how that self was invented, why it is so exhausting, and the older answer the modern one replaced. Identity not as an achievement you assemble but as a gift you receive, made in the image of God, given a name in Christ you cannot lose, and finally secure enough to be spent in love rather than performed for a verdict. It is honest about the tiredness, honest about the skeptic's objections, and it never shames the people worn out by performing. Built so any volunteer can lead it with no prep. Come tired, not finished.

promoKit.inviteCaption: The age told you to look inward, build a self, and perform it for approval forever, and it is exhausting. A five-session study on who you are, walking out of the project of self-creation and into an identity you did not have to manufacture and cannot lose, made in God's image and given a name in Christ. Honest about the tiredness, honest about the skeptic's questions, and it never shames the people worn out by performing. Come tired, not finished.
quoteCards: The self you are told to be true to was itself invented. It is a floor someone built, and they are telling you it is the ground.
You become two people at once, the author writing the self and the anxious audience watching to see if it sells, and both jobs run all day with no shift change.
The exhaustion is not a sign you are building the self badly. It is a sign you were never meant to build one at all.
Your worth was settled at creation, by God's act, not computed fresh each morning from the day's results.
You cannot achieve your way to the thing you most need, because the thing you most need was always a gift.
There is a name that holds when everything you built collapses, and it is not a name you made.
When his own performance and feelings gave way, Luther returned to a fact done to him. I am baptized.
You cannot pour out a self you are still desperately trying to fill.
The self you finally stop clutching, the self you pour out in love, is not the self you lose. It is the only one you ever truly find.
Not the self you were sold. The self you were given, and then, freely, gave away.
